questions.title: How do FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) and OSC § 1216(a)(3) interact, and can OSC investigate without meeting § 552's predicates?
questions.question_body: I’m reading this opinion and am confused about the relationship between § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) and § 1216(a)(3). The court says OSC can pursue a FOIA investigation under § 1216 even though the three predicates of § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) are not satisfied. But my notes say § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) triggers OSC’s action. Does OSC have a ‘mandatory’ investigative duty under § 1216 independent of § 552? How does the statutory structure explain this relationship?

questions.title: Does OSC's enforcement discretion under § 1214(c) and § 1216(c) allow a court to compel it to investigate a FOIA violation?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that OSC disclaimed authority because the predicates of § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) were unmet and that § 1216(c) cements the decision to investigate or not as discretionary. I’m unsure whether a federal court can compel OSC to conduct a § 1216 investigation. If OSC has no ‘mandatory’ obligation, what limits the court’s ability to intervene? Is there any precedent that a court can force OSC to conduct a § 1216 investigation?

questions.title: Why does the court deny AFL standing based on an informational injury from DOJ’s non‑compliance with a FOIA request?
questions.question_body: AFL claimed injury from DOJ withholding records, yet the appellate court says that doesn’t create standing. The district court found the FOIA request was denied. However, the appellate court states the injury is not concrete because any informational injury flows directly from DOJ, not OSC. I’m puzzled: if the relief seeks to compel OSC to investigate, how is the plaintiff’s injury linked to OSC? Did the court view the informational injury as too speculative or is there a residual standard for informational standing?

questions.title: What distinguishes a procedural injury from a substantive injury under Article III standing, and how does that apply to AFL’s claim?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses ‘procedural injury’ and ‘procedural right in vacuo’ and mentions relaxed standing rules for procedural injury (e.g., Ctr. for Law & Educ.). I’m not clear on how the courts separate procedural vs substantive injuries. Does a violation of a procedural right automatically make the injury procedural, or does it depend on the nature of the impediment? And how does that determination affect AFL’s standing claim under § 1216?

questions.title: How does the relaxed standing standard for procedural rights apply to § 1216 investigations, and why is it insufficient for AFL?
questions.question_body: The appellate court notes that for procedural rights the court relaxes standards of imminence and redressability. Yet AFL still failed to satisfy ‘injury in fact’ and causation. How do we apply the ‘relaxed’ standard in a case where the alleged injury is protected by a procedural right? Why doesn’t the mere threat of losing procedural protections count as a concrete injury sufficient for standing?

questions.title: Does a procedural right in vacuo—such as OSC’s privilege to investigate—constitute a concrete injury, or must the plaintiff have an actual entitlement to information to have standing?
questions.question_body: The court said a procedural right in vacuo is insufficient, citing Summers v. Earth Island. How does that principle operate? If AFL’s only claim is that OSC should investigate, does that itself constitute an injury, or does it need to lead to a tangible benefit (e.g., notice, information)? Are there any cases that clarify when a procedural right alone is enough for Article III standing?

questions.title: How do courts analyze causation and redressability when an agency’s discretionary decision could indirectly affect a plaintiff’s FOIA right?
questions.question_body: The appellate court’s reasoning was that the causal chain from OSC’s lack of investigation to DOJ’s eventual release of records involved speculation about two independent agencies. I’m confused about the test for causal connection here. Is speculation about what other agencies might do unacceptable, and what standard determines whether redressability is satisfied? How does the court decide if a favorable judgment here would ‘very likely spur the next steps necessary to redress’ the plaintiff’s injury?
